title: Making plans together
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: ¿A qué hora? — A las + <number> + y media/cuarto

rules.text: The we-form ends in -amos, -emos or -imos: hablamos, comemos, podemos. It is the last person the course was missing, and vamos — which M6 of the level below already taught — is its irregular star.
A suggestion is the plain we-form, said as a question: ¿Vamos al cine? English needs "shall we" or "let's" and Spanish has no equivalent to translate — reaching for one produces nothing that works.

A settled arrangement is spoken in the PRESENT: Mañana como con mi hermana. English does the same with its own present continuous, so the habit transfers; the time word carries the future, not the verb.
The clock counts up to the half hour with y: a las ocho y media, a las nueve y cuarto. Past the half hour Spanish counts down with menos, which this course leaves to M9.
A day takes el: el sábado, el viernes. With the article it can mean either this coming one or every one, and the sentence decides.

sentences.cue: Shall we go to the cinema tomorrow?

words.note: Masculine: el cine, and a plus el fuses to al. The word is the building and the art form alike.

sentences.trap: No word for "shall" and none for "let's". The we-form said as a question is the whole suggestion.
sentences.sound: SI-ne in Latin America, THI-ne in most of Spain. Both are standard and neither is a mistake.

variations.cue: Shall we go to the square?
variations.changed: a feminine place, so no fusion happens

variations.cue: Shall we go to the cinema on Saturday?
variations.changed: a day instead of mañana

variations.cue: We're going to the cinema tonight.
variations.changed: said flat, it stops being a suggestion and becomes a plan

mistake.why: a and el always fuse: al cine. There is no situation in which they stand apart.

sentences.usage: The everyday invitation among friends. The question mark does all the work.
sentences.mnemonic: Ask the we-form and you have suggested something.

sentences.cue: Do you want to eat with me on Saturday?

words.note: con and mí fused into one word, and it is the only place that happens: conmigo, contigo. con él and con mi hermana stay two words.

sentences.trap: con mí is not Spanish. The two words have grown together and there is no way to pull them apart.
sentences.sound: kon-MI-go, stressed in the middle, and said as one word because it is one.

variations.cue: Do you want to eat with me tomorrow?
variations.changed: tomorrow instead of a named day

variations.cue: I want to eat with you.
variations.changed: the other fused form, said as a statement

variations.cue: Do you want to meet up with me on Friday?
variations.changed: a different thing to do together

mistake.why: con and mí fuse: conmigo. The unfused version does not exist.

sentences.usage: An invitation to one person. Warmer than ¿Vamos…?, because it names who you want there.
sentences.mnemonic: Two words that never learnt to stand apart.

words.note: The we-form of poder, and the stem does NOT change: podemos, not puedemos, because the stress falls on the ending. The row for poder is M1's.
To arrange to meet, and it has no single English word — "meet up" is the nearest. It is the verb every plan in Spain is made with.

sentences.trap: podemos breaks the ue you learnt in M1, and it breaks it for a reason: the stress has moved off the stem.
sentences.sound: po-DE-mos. Hearing the o rather than the ue is how you know the person changed.

variations.cue: We can meet up on Friday.
variations.changed: a day rather than an hour

variations.cue: We can eat at home.
variations.changed: a different thing to do, same frame

variations.cue: We can't meet up tomorrow.
variations.changed: the refusal, with no in front

mistake.why: The stem only changes when the stress lands on it. In the we-form it does not: podemos.

sentences.usage: How a plan gets made rather than suggested. Podemos offers without pressing.
sentences.mnemonic: Stress moves off the stem and the ue goes with it.

words.note: The we-form of quedar, and the same word is the question and the answer: ¿Quedamos a las ocho? — Quedamos a las ocho. The row for quedar is S03's.

sentences.trap: The same form asks and settles. Spanish needs no extra word to turn the suggestion into the arrangement.
sentences.sound: ke-DA-mos. The stress is on the middle syllable, as it is in podemos.

variations.cue: Where shall we meet?
variations.changed: the place rather than the time

variations.cue: Shall we meet on Saturday?
variations.changed: the whole question in three words

variations.cue: We'll meet in the square.
variations.changed: the answer, and en for the place

mistake.why: The present does the job: ¿A qué hora quedamos? A future tense here sounds like a forecast rather than a plan.

sentences.usage: The second message of any plan. The first one proposed it; this one pins it down.
sentences.mnemonic: One form, and it both asks and agrees.

words.note: Feminine because the hour is: las ocho y media. It counts up from the hour just said, so this is half past eight and never half past seven.

sentences.trap: Spanish counts up to the half hour and English says "past". The hour named is the one already struck.
sentences.sound: ME-dya, two syllables, with the i gliding into the a.

variations.cue: At half past ten.
variations.changed: a different hour, same half

variations.display: Quedamos a las ocho y media.
variations.cue: We'll meet at half past eight.
variations.changed: the time inside the plan

variations.display: ¿A las ocho y media, en la plaza?
variations.cue: Half past eight, in the square?
variations.changed: time and place in one question

mistake.why: media agrees with the feminine hora hiding behind las: y media.

sentences.usage: Half past is the commonest time anyone arranges anything for.
sentences.mnemonic: The hour you name is the one already gone.

words.note: The ue glides as it does in puedo and nuevo. It never changes shape.
Masculine here, unlike media, because it is a quarter of an hour and not a half of one: y cuarto. It is also the word for a room, and the sentence says which.

sentences.trap: media is feminine and cuarto is masculine, in the same frame. There is no rule joining them; they are two words that behave differently.
sentences.sound: NWE-ve, KWAR-to — both with the same glide, one after the other.

variations.cue: At quarter past ten.
variations.changed: another hour

variations.cue: Shall we meet at quarter past nine?
variations.changed: the time inside the question

variations.cue: At half past nine.
variations.changed: the half hour of the same hour

mistake.why: cuarto does not agree with the hour: y cuarto, always. media does, and that asymmetry is simply how it is.

sentences.usage: Quarter past is arranged; quarter to needs menos, which this course leaves to M9.

words.note: Spain's agreement word, said constantly and about anything. Mexico says sale and much of Latin America says está bien; all three are understood everywhere.
Already ends in -s in the singular, like lunes and martes, so the plural changes only the article: el viernes, los viernes.

sentences.trap: viernes is not a plural. The days ending in -s look plural and are not, until the article says otherwise.
sentences.sound: BA-le, with a b sound at the start — Spanish v and b are the same letter to the ear.

variations.cue: OK, see you tomorrow.
variations.changed: tomorrow instead of a named day

variations.cue: OK, see you Saturday.
variations.changed: the other way of signing off with a day

variations.cue: OK, we'll meet at eight.
variations.changed: agreement followed by the arrangement itself

mistake.why: los viernes means every Friday. For this coming one it is el viernes.

sentences.usage: The last message of the exchange. In Spain vale ends almost every plan ever made.
sentences.mnemonic: el for this one, los for every one.

sentences.cue: I'm eating with my sister tomorrow.

words.note: The plain present, doing the future's job. The row is L1-M4's; what is new is that mañana in front of it is enough to make the sentence a plan.

sentences.trap: No future tense anywhere, and none is needed. The time word carries it, exactly as English's "I'm eating tomorrow" does.
sentences.sound: KO-mo, and it is not M2's cómo — that one has an accent and asks a question.

variations.display: El sábado como con mi hermano.
variations.cue: I'm eating with my brother on Saturday.
variations.changed: a named day, and the other sibling

variations.cue: I'm going to the cinema tomorrow.
variations.changed: another verb in the same arrangement present

variations.cue: I'm not eating at home tomorrow.
variations.changed: the negative, and a place instead of a person

mistake.why: The accent turns it into the question word. como eats; cómo asks how.

sentences.usage: A settled plan, stated rather than proposed. The listener is being told, not asked.
sentences.mnemonic: Put a time in front and the present becomes a plan.

sentences.literal: The Sunday for the afternoon, OK?

words.note: Unlike viernes it takes a plural -s: los domingos. Days are not capitalised in Spanish.

sentences.trap: No capital letter. Days, months and languages are all lower case in Spanish, and capitalising them is the most visible English habit there is.
sentences.sound: do-MIN-go, with a hard g, and the n fully said before it.

variations.cue: Sunday morning, OK?
variations.changed: the other end of the day

variations.cue: Friday night.
variations.changed: a different day and a different part of it

variations.cue: On Sundays I eat at home.
variations.changed: the plural, which turns one day into every one

mistake.why: domingo is not capitalised. Nor is any day, month or language in Spanish.

sentences.usage: Half a plan, offered for agreement. ¿vale? at the end is how Spain asks whether that suits you.
sentences.mnemonic: Lower case, always — the days are just words.

sentences.display: El fin de semana no puedo, lo siento.
sentences.cue: I can't at the weekend, I'm sorry.
sentences.literal: The end of week not I-can, it I-feel.

words.note: Three words as one: the end of the week. Masculine, because fin is: el fin de semana.

sentences.trap: Spanish spells out what English compresses into one word. There is no single word for weekend.
sentences.sound: The three run together — fin-de-se-MA-na — with one stress, on the last word.

variations.display: El fin de semana voy al cine.
variations.cue: I'm going to the cinema at the weekend.
variations.changed: a plan rather than a refusal

variations.display: El fin de semana no puedo quedar.
variations.cue: I can't meet up at the weekend.
variations.changed: the refusal with the verb named

variations.display: El domingo no puedo, lo siento.
variations.cue: I can't on Sunday, I'm sorry.
variations.changed: one day instead of the whole weekend

mistake.display: La fin de semana no puedo.
mistake.why: fin is masculine, so it is el fin de semana.

sentences.usage: Turning an invitation down. Adding lo siento is what keeps it warm, and it is expected.
sentences.mnemonic: The end of the week, spelled out.

comprehensionPool.cue: Shall we go to the cinema tomorrow?
Do you want to eat with me on Saturday?
I'm eating with my sister tomorrow.

comprehensionPool.display: El fin de semana no puedo, lo siento.
comprehensionPool.cue: I can't at the weekend, I'm sorry.
We can meet up on Sunday.
